subtopic_detail: pregnant childcare worker exposed to a slapped cheek rash outbreak at work in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. She works in a childcare centre where three children developed a bright red rash across both cheeks last week, and she has been told to see a doctor. She had face to face contact with all three children in the two days before their rashes appeared.

She feels well and has no rash, fever or joint pains. Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated. Her booking bloods showed her to be rubella immune, varicella immune and negative for syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus, and her blood group is O positive. Her 12 week ultrasound was consistent with dates and showed no abnormality. Examination today is unremarkable with a soft non tender abdomen, a symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, and a foetal heart rate of 148 beats per minute on handheld Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling
data_table.Booking investigations: Rubella immune, varicella immune, negative syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology, blood group O positive
data_table.Imaging: Twelve week ultrasound consistent with dates and structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange weekly middle cerebral artery Doppler studies from now until 30 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is exactly the right surveillance once maternal infection is confirmed, and it is what detects foetal anaemia. Starting it before serology commits an already immune woman to fourteen weeks of unnecessary scans. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that maternal infection at this gestation carries no risk to the pregnancy
options.rationale: The risk is real between about 9 and 20 weeks, when the foetal liver is the main site of erythropoiesis and red cell lifespan is short, which is precisely the window she is in. Vertical transmission occurs in around a third of maternal infections. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for amniocentesis with viral polymerase chain reaction on the amniotic fluid sample
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid testing confirms foetal infection but is invasive and is reserved for cases where foetal anaemia or hydrops is already suspected on ultrasound. It is not a screening test after an exposure. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Offer intravenous immunoglobulin within 72 hours of the exposure to prevent transmission
options.rationale: Post exposure immunoglobulin is effective for varicella and for measles but there is no established prophylaxis against parvovirus B19 in pregnancy. Offering it implies a protection that does not exist. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Send maternal immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result
options.rationale: Around 60 per cent of Australian women of childbearing age are already immune to parvovirus B19, so serology first establishes whether she is at any risk at all before committing to surveillance. Immunoglobulin G positive with immunoglobulin M negative means past infection and needs nothing further. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, and childcare and primary school staff are the classic occupational exposure group. Infected children are contagious in the week before the rash appears and are no longer infectious once it is visible, so exposure has usually already occurred by the time an outbreak is recognised. Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the highest foetal risk because the virus targets erythroid precursors, and the foetus of that gestation has rapid red cell turnover and limited marrow reserve, producing anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Vertical transmission occurs in roughly a third of maternal infections and hydrops develops in a few per cent, typically two to six weeks after maternal infection. Management after a confirmed maternal infection is serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity measurement, and intrauterine transfusion where anaemia is detected, which achieves good survival.
key_points: Children are infectious before the rash appears, not after it.
About 60 per cent of women of childbearing age are already immune, so test serology first.
Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the greatest risk of foetal anaemia and hydrops.
Confirmed infection is followed with serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity.
Intrauterine transfusion treats detected foetal anaemia with good survival.
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median for gestational age is the threshold that triggers referral for foetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion, and it detects significant anaemia non invasively with sensitivity above 90 per cent.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

subtopic_detail: postmenopausal woman with a glazed red vestibule, lacy white streaks and a narrowing vaginal opening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman with two years of vulval soreness, a raw burning feeling and a yellow stained discharge. She has been treated with six separate courses of topical and oral antifungal therapy and one course of topical oestrogen without benefit, and intercourse has become impossible.

She went through menopause at 51 and has no other medical problems. She mentions in passing that the inside of her cheeks has been sore and that her dentist commented on some white lines there. On examination the labia minora have partly fused anteriorly and the vaginal opening admits only one fingertip. The vestibule is a glazed bright red with a sharply demarcated edge, and at the margin of the erythema there is a fine lacy white network. There is no white parchment like change over the labia and perineum and no ecchymosis. A vaginal pH is 6.0 and a vaginal swab is negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.

data_table.Examination: Glazed sharply demarcated vestibular erythema with a lacy white reticular border, partial anterior labial fusion, introitus admitting one fingertip
data_table.Oral: Reticular white striae on the buccal mucosa with associated soreness
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 6.0, swab negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of oral fluconazole taken as a weekly maintenance dose
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is used for recurrent candidiasis, which she does not have on repeated swabs and which does not fuse the labia or narrow the introitus. Six failed courses should already have prompted a change of diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the adhesions with vaginal dilator therapy started afterwards
options.rationale: Surgery has a place once the inflammatory disease is controlled, because operating on actively inflamed tissue leads to rapid re adhesion through the same process that caused the fusion. Medical control comes first, with dilators used as an adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid for lichen sclerosus and review in three months
options.rationale: The treatment is right but the diagnosis is the near pair that gets confused: lichen sclerosus gives white parchment like atrophic skin over the labia, perineum and perianal area in a figure of eight, with ecchymosis and fissuring, and it spares the vagina. Erosive lichen planus involves the vestibule and vagina and produces the reticular border seen here. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence long term topical oestrogen therapy
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which produces a uniformly pale thin friable epithelium rather than a sharply demarcated erosion with a reticular border. She has already failed a course of it, which argues against that diagnosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Glazed erosive vestibular erythema with a lacy reticular border and matching buccal striae is erosive lichen planus, which is confirmed histologically and treated with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid. Biopsy also establishes a baseline because the condition carries a malignant potential. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Erosive lichen planus is an immune mediated mucocutaneous disease that affects the vulva, vagina and mouth and is the most disabling of the vulval dermatoses. The vulvovaginal gingival syndrome describes the combination of erosive vulval and vaginal disease with desquamative gingivitis, and asking about the mouth often unlocks a diagnosis that has been missed for years. The physical signs that separate it from lichen sclerosus are its involvement of the vestibule and vagina, the glazed erosive surface, the lacy white reticular Wickham striae at the border, and the raised vaginal pH from the associated vaginitis. Untreated disease causes progressive scarring with labial resorption, introital narrowing and vaginal stenosis, and it carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk of the order of one to three per cent. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol, with calcineurin inhibitors, vaginal preparations or systemic immunosuppression added for resistant disease, and long term surveillance is required.
key_points: Erosive lichen planus involves the vagina and vestibule; lichen sclerosus spares the vagina.
A lacy white reticular border and oral striae are the discriminating findings.
Repeated failed antifungal courses should prompt reassessment of the diagnosis.
Biopsy from the edge of the lesion confirms the diagnosis and establishes a baseline.
Scarring causes labial fusion and vaginal stenosis, and malignant transformation can occur.
explanation.pearls: A vaginal pH above 4.5 in a woman with vulval symptoms points to vaginal involvement, which occurs in erosive lichen planus and desquamative inflammatory vaginitis but essentially never in lichen sclerosus, so a strip of indicator paper separates the two dermatoses at the bedside.

subtopic_detail: woman who never established milk supply and has had no periods since a delivery needing massive transfusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman nine months after the birth of her second child. She has come about persistent tiredness, feeling cold all the time and dizziness when she stands up quickly. Her periods have not returned and she is using condoms for contraception.

Her delivery was complicated by bleeding requiring eight units of red cells and a return to theatre, and she spent two days in intensive care. She tells you she was never able to produce any milk at all despite considerable support from the lactation service, and that her pubic and axillary hair has thinned. She stopped breastfeeding attempts at three weeks and the baby has thrived on formula. On examination she looks pale with fine dry skin, her blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, her pulse is 64 beats per minute and she is afebrile. Sodium is 128 mmol/L (135 to 145) and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees
data_table.Examination: Pale fine dry skin, thinning axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation of palmar creases or buccal mucosa
data_table.Obstetric history: Postpartum haemorrhage requiring eight units of red cells, return to theatre and intensive care admission
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request an early morning cortisol with paired anterior pituitary and thyroid hormone levels
options.rationale: Failure of lactation and amenorrhoea after a haemorrhage needing massive transfusion, with postural hypotension and hyponatraemia, is Sheehan syndrome from pituitary infarction. A combined anterior pituitary panel with a morning cortisol identifies which axes have failed and how urgently replacement is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Request a nine item depression questionnaire with thyroid function and vitamin B12 levels
options.rationale: Screening for postnatal depression is appropriate in any tired new mother and the overlap of symptoms is real. It does not account for absent lactation, postural hypotension, loss of body hair or hyponatraemia, all of which are endocrine findings. (Source: COPE: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Request a short synacthen test with adrenal antibodies and plasma renin activity
options.rationale: This workup is directed at primary adrenal insufficiency, the near pair, which is distinguished by hyperpigmentation, hyperkalaemia and a raised adrenocorticotrophic hormone because the adrenal itself has failed. Normal potassium and no pigmentation point to a secondary cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request a serum prolactin with a follicle stimulating hormone and a transvaginal ultrasound
options.rationale: This combination investigates secondary amenorrhoea from a prolactinoma or premature ovarian insufficiency and would be reasonable if amenorrhoea were the only problem. It misses the adrenal and thyroid axes, and it is the cortisol deficiency here that is potentially fatal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Request thyroid stimulating hormone alone with a full blood count and iron studies
options.rationale: This panel targets postpartum thyroiditis and iron deficiency, which are far commoner causes of postnatal fatigue and are worth having. In pituitary failure the thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal or low despite a low free thyroxine, so measuring it alone gives false reassurance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary caused by severe postpartum haemorrhage and hypotension, made possible by the physiological enlargement of the lactotroph rich gland during pregnancy within a fixed bony fossa. Presentation is often delayed by months or years because the deficiencies accumulate gradually, and the two earliest and most specific clues are failure to lactate and failure of menses to return. Anterior pituitary hormones are typically lost in a characteristic order, with growth hormone and gonadotrophins going first, then adrenocorticotrophic hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone, while the posterior pituitary is usually spared. Hyponatraemia is common and reflects cortisol deficiency impairing free water excretion rather than true salt loss. The diagnosis matters because unrecognised secondary adrenal insufficiency can present as adrenal crisis during an intercurrent illness, and glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating one.
key_points: Failure of lactation plus failure of menses to return after major haemorrhage is the hallmark.
Presentation is frequently delayed by months to years after the index birth.
In secondary hypothyroidism the thyroid stimulating hormone is normal or low, not raised.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium suggests a secondary rather than primary adrenal cause.
Replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Starting thyroxine before hydrocortisone in any form of hypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis within days, because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance, so the order of replacement is not a matter of preference.

subtopic_detail: woman whose device threads cannot be seen and whose uterine cavity is empty on transvaginal scanning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who cannot feel the threads of her copper intrauterine device. It was inserted eight months ago at six weeks postpartum while she was fully breastfeeding, and the threads were checked and documented as visible at her six week review after insertion.

Her periods returned four months ago and have been regular since, with no unusually heavy loss and no episode of severe cramping that she recalls. She has had no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. A urinary pregnancy test today is negative. On speculum examination no threads are visible at the external os and the cervix looks normal. Gentle exploration of the cervical canal with a thread retriever finds nothing. A transvaginal ultrasound performed in the practice reports an empty uterine cavity with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm, no intrauterine device identified, and normal ovaries with no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: No threads visible at the external os, normal cervix, non tender mobile uterus of normal size
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterine cavity, endometrial thickness 6 mm, no device identified, normal ovaries, no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, insertion at six weeks postpartum during full breastfeeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient hysteroscopy to inspect the cavity and retrieve the device directly
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is used when the device is known to be intrauterine but embedded or with retracted threads, which is the near pair here. A cavity already shown to be empty on ultrasound will simply be confirmed as empty, and the device is not inside it. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Refer directly for a diagnostic laparoscopy to locate and retrieve the migrated device
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is the correct retrieval procedure once an intra abdominal device is confirmed, and it is what she will need if the film is positive. Operating before localising the device commits her to an anaesthetic that is unnecessary if it was simply expelled. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound before considering any further imaging modality
options.rationale: Transabdominal scanning widens the field beyond the transvaginal view and is a reasonable adjunct, but a device that has migrated into the upper abdomen or omentum lies outside the pelvic field and is easily missed on ultrasound of any window. Radiography covers the whole cavity in one image. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Reassure her that the device has been expelled and reinsert a new device at this visit
options.rationale: Expulsion is the commoner of the two outcomes and she has had regular periods since, which makes this genuinely tempting. Reinserting without excluding an intra abdominal device leaves a perforated device in the peritoneal cavity where it can cause adhesions or bowel injury. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange a plain abdominal radiograph covering the diaphragm to the pelvic floor
options.rationale: An empty uterus on ultrasound has two explanations, expulsion and perforation, and they cannot be distinguished clinically because up to a third of perforations are painless. A plain film of the whole abdomen and pelvis is the test that finds or excludes a migrated radio opaque device. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

explanation.summary: Missing intrauterine device threads is a common presentation and the assessment follows a fixed sequence: exclude pregnancy, look in the canal, image the uterus, and if the cavity is empty, image the abdomen. Where ultrasound shows no device in the uterus, the two possibilities are expulsion, which occurs in about one in twenty users and is commonest in the first year, and uterine perforation, which occurs in around one to two per thousand insertions. Perforation risk is increased roughly six fold by insertion while breastfeeding and is also higher when insertion occurs within six months of delivery, because the uterus is soft and involuting. Critically, perforation is silent in a substantial minority, so a painless history and normal subsequent periods do not exclude it, and a plain abdominal radiograph is mandatory before a replacement device is inserted. A confirmed intra abdominal device is retrieved laparoscopically because copper in particular incites an inflammatory reaction with adhesions and occasional bowel or bladder erosion.
key_points: Sequence is pregnancy test, canal inspection, pelvic ultrasound, then abdominal radiograph.
An empty cavity means either expulsion or perforation, which cannot be told apart clinically.
Breastfeeding at insertion and insertion within six months of delivery both raise perforation risk.
Up to a third of perforations are asymptomatic, so a painless history excludes nothing.
Never reinsert a device until the abdominal film has excluded a migrated one.
explanation.pearls: Both copper and levonorgestrel devices are radio opaque, so a single plain abdominal film from diaphragm to pelvic floor answers the question in minutes; the common error is limiting the film to the pelvis, which misses devices that have migrated into the omentum or upper abdomen.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: Intrauterine contraception

subtopic_detail: young woman with patchy scalp hair loss admitting to pulling hairs out when studying under pressure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student who has noticed thinning over the top and right side of her scalp for the past year. She wears her hair up to disguise it. With some embarrassment she tells you that she pulls hairs out one at a time, mostly in the evenings while studying, and feels a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards.

She says she is not trying to hurt herself and does not want to die. She does not eat the hair. She has always been a worrier but has no low mood, no weight change and sleeps reasonably well. On examination there are ill defined patches of shortened hair of varying lengths over the vertex and right parietal scalp, with no scaling, erythema, scarring or pustules, and the underlying skin looks normal. Eyebrows and eyelashes are intact. Thyroid function, iron studies and a full blood examination arranged by a colleague last month were all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Ill defined patches of hair of varying lengths over the vertex and right parietal scalp, no scaling, scarring, erythema or pustules
data_table.Distribution: Eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no body hair loss, no nail changes
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, iron studies and full blood examination all within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic with reactive affect, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence sertraline titrated to a therapeutic dose and review her response in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder, which trichotillomania sits alongside in the diagnostic grouping, so the reasoning is understandable. Trials in trichotillomania itself have been largely negative, which is why it is not first line. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine at a low dose with monitoring of weight and metabolic parameters
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics have some trial support in refractory cases and so are a real third line option rather than a nonsense answer. Starting one before any behavioural therapy exposes a nineteen year old to metabolic risk she does not need to take yet. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid to the affected areas and review her in eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats alopecia areata, the dermatological near pair, which produces smooth completely bald patches with exclamation mark hairs rather than broken hairs of differing lengths. There is no inflammatory process here to suppress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Arrange a scalp biopsy to distinguish scarring from non scarring patterns of alopecia
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for scalp hair loss where the clinical pattern is genuinely uncertain or scarring is suspected from erythema, scale or loss of follicular openings. A clear account of pulling with normal scalp skin makes the diagnosis without histology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training delivered by a psychologist experienced in this technique
options.rationale: Hairs of varying lengths in non scarring patches with premonitory tension and relief on pulling is trichotillomania, and habit reversal training is the intervention with the strongest evidence base. It combines awareness training with a competing response and is more effective than any medication studied. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders and involves recurrent pulling out of one's own hair with repeated attempts to stop, causing distress or impairment. Onset is typically in early adolescence and it is far more often reported by females in clinical samples. The scalp is the commonest site, followed by eyebrows and eyelashes, and the examination finding that distinguishes it from alopecia areata is hairs of differing lengths within irregular non scarring patches on normal underlying skin. Many patients describe a premonitory urge with tension relieved by pulling, while others pull automatically without awareness during sedentary activities, and the two patterns often coexist. Habit reversal training is first line, often within a broader cognitive behavioural framework, and N acetylcysteine has some supportive trial evidence as an adjunct; comorbid anxiety and depression should be treated on their own merits.
key_points: Hairs of varying lengths on normal non scarred skin distinguish it from alopecia areata.
Premonitory tension with relief after pulling is characteristic but not universal.
It is classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders, not with self harm.
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication.
Ask about trichophagia, because swallowed hair can form a gastric bezoar.
explanation.pearls: Always ask whether the patient swallows the hair, because trichophagia can produce a trichobezoar extending through the pylorus into the small bowel, which presents with an epigastric mass and obstruction and needs surgical removal.
